Why does probe platinization improve SVET signal quality?

Electrodepositing platinum black onto the probe tip dramatically increases its electrochemical surface area, creating a highly capacitive interface (target >1 nF) that reduces impedance and lowers noise in the measured signal.

Why does excessive platinization degrade SVET probe performance?

When the hairy platinum black structure becomes too thick, it fills in on itself, reducing the effective surface area and causing signal instability and increased noise rather than further improvement.
Why does the SVET probe need to vibrate during measurement?

Vibration converts the DC potential gradient above the sample into an AC signal at a known frequency, enabling phase-sensitive lock-in detection that extracts the signal from background noise with approximately 10x better signal-to-noise ratio than static SRET.

Why does increasing electrolyte conductivity reduce SVET signal strength?

In high-conductivity solutions, ionic currents produce smaller potential gradients in the electrolyte above the sample, so the voltage difference sensed by the vibrating probe decreases, reducing sensitivity and raising the detection threshold.
Why must the probe-sample distance be at least 4 times the vibration amplitude?

If the standoff distance is less than 4x the vibration amplitude, the probe spends part of its oscillation cycle meaningfully closer to the surface than assumed, distorting the sinusoidal position signal that the lock-in amplifier relies on and causing overestimation of local currents.

Why does increasing probe-sample distance reduce SVET spatial resolution?

Spatial resolution in SVET is limited by the probe height above the sample, because current from a point source spreads laterally as it travels upward, meaning two adjacent corrosion sites can only be resolved if the probe height is approximately half their separation distance.
Why is the lock-in amplifier phase angle setting critical in SVET?

The lock-in must be set so that the probe's motion-induced voltage appears fully in-phase with the reference signal, because a 90-degree phase offset causes the output to go to zero, meaning an incorrect phase setting can make real electrochemical signals disappear entirely from the measurement.

What is the recommended probe-sample distance during SVET calibration on the AE system in 10 mM NaCl, and why is it used as the standard?

The recommended probe-sample distance for AE SVET calibration in 10 mM NaCl is 150 µm, providing a balance between sufficient signal strength and safe standoff from the surface, and this distance is used as the reference height when applying the −60 nA calibration current to convert the measured gradient into current density.
What gain configuration is used in the AE SVET system, and why should the pre-amplifier gain not be altered?

The standard AE SVET configuration uses 500x gain in the PSDA-2 and 100x in the pre-amplifier, and the pre-amplifier gain must not be altered without updating the matching gain setting in the ASET-LV4 software SENSOR window, because a mismatch causes the current densities reported by the software to be incorrect.
Why is 10 mM NaCl the standard solution used for AE SVET probe calibration?

10 mM NaCl is used for AE SVET calibration because it provides a well-defined, reproducible conductivity that is low enough to generate measurable potential gradients during the Point Injection Source calibration procedure while being representative of dilute corrosion-relevant electrolyte conditions.

What sandpaper grit is recommended for preparing Pt wire surfaces before platinization in the AE system?

Fine-grit sandpaper (typically 500–600 grit) is used to abrade platinum wire surfaces before platinization in the AE SVET system to remove surface contamination and create a clean, lightly roughened surface that promotes uniform adhesion of the platinum black deposit.
What compressed gas and pressure are recommended for probe vibration calibration and environmental cleaning in the AE SVET setup?

text: What artifact results from using a vibration amplitude greater than 25 µm in SVET?

Vibration amplitudes exceeding 25 µm cause local electrolyte stirring that thins the diffusion layer around the probe tip, artificially enhancing oxygen transport to cathodic sites and leading to significant overestimation of total cathodic currents relative to true anodic current.

text: What is the consequence for SVET data if the electrolyte evaporates significantly during a long scan?

Electrolyte evaporation during long SVET scans progressively increases solution conductivity, which reduces the potential gradients above the sample and causes the measured current density values to be systematically underestimated over the course of the experiment.
What happens to probe performance if the platinization current stops increasing early during the deposition process?

If the platinization current stops increasing prematurely, it indicates that the platinum black deposit has overfilled the hairy surface structure, reducing the effective electrochemical surface area and resulting in a probe with excessive noise and insufficient capacitance for reliable SVET measurements.

text: What is the key advantage of SVET over LEIS and SDC when studying certain sample types?

Unlike LEIS and SDC, which require a direct electrical connection to the sample, SVET can characterize naturally active, freely corroding, or biological samples because it measures ionic current in the overlying solution without any physical contact or external electrical bias.

text: How does SVET spatial resolution compare to the physical probe tip diameter, and why?

SVET spatial resolution is primarily determined by the probe standoff distance rather than the tip diameter, because current spreads laterally as it travels upward through the electrolyte, meaning using a smaller tip does not improve resolution once the tip height significantly exceeds the feature size being mapped.
Why is the LECC-SVET approach considered more quantitatively accurate than standard SVET, and who developed it?

LECC-SVET, introduced by Saeedikhani et al. (2022), replaces bulk electrolyte conductivity with locally simulated conductivity values derived from finite element modeling of the diffusion layer, yielding current density estimates closer to true unperturbed corrosion conditions than those obtained using bulk conductivity.
What fundamental limitation prevents SVET from distinguishing between different electrochemical reactions occurring at the same cathodic site?

SVET measures only the magnitude and direction of ionic current density in solution and has no chemical specificity, so it cannot differentiate between, for example, oxygen reduction and hydrogen evolution occurring simultaneously at the same cathodic region without complementary chemical sensing techniques.
Why is a mirror used during SVET probe vibration calibration in the AE system?

The mirror is used to visually confirm the probe vibration amplitude under magnification by observing the reflected image of the oscillating probe tip, allowing the operator to verify that the actual mechanical displacement matches the software-set amplitude before beginning measurements.
Why is the electrode assembly turned upside down during the filling step of glass microelectrode preparation?

Turning the electrode assembly upside down during the filling step is an acceptable practice in the AE SVET system that allows working solution to be introduced via syringe into the glass capillary housing the Ag/AgCl microelectrode, helping ensure complete filling without trapped air pockets.
Why must the P-47 pipette puller be used for fabricating glass microelectrodes in the AE SVET system?

The P-47 pipette puller is used in the AE SVET system to fabricate glass microelectrodes by running Program 4 at a ramp test temperature of 607 °C to pull the glass capillary to the fine-tipped geometry required for the glass microelectrode assembly.
